messages.author: e522eb447f9e62f8
messages.subject: R, Hebrew, and PDFs
parts:
Hi all,

I'm a newbie in the group (and to working with R in Hebrew), and am
looking for a little help.

I'm using R to analyze some data: In my script, I've sunk the console
output and redirected the graphical output to a pdf. (There are
multiple graphs which is handled quite nicely by R when redirected
using pdf().)

The problem is that R doesn't seem to have postscript/pdf support for
Hebrew fonts, so all my labels come out in "Greek". I've written a
look-up table to deal with the graph titles, but this is by no means a
complete or even useful solution.

Any ideas? Is there a postscript file out there I can stick in the
right directory that R can use? Is there some other package that can
help me out of this hole?

I'm trying very hard not to cave in and switch to SAS; I really like
R.

Thank you!

Ari

N.B. I found an R News publication where they wrote, "Font support for
R graphics devices is equally difficult and has currently only been
achieved on Windows and on comprehensively equipped X servers. In
particular, postscript() and pdf() are restricted to Western and
Eastern European languages as the commonly-available fonts are (and
some are restricted to ISO 8859-1)." I suppose I'm now hoping that
someone found a workaround over the last 7 years. I'm pretty sure that
Japanese is now possible. (See: http://www.r-project.org/doc/Rnews/Rnews_2005-1.pdf,
page 5.)

הכל יושב בצהלנט

All the variable names are in Hebrew; the factor labels are also in
Hebrew.
A plot() request produces a title, axis labels, and factor labels
which are all perfectly

tiff, bmp, etc.

however, is accurate;

parts:
סליחה שאני מתפרץ לדיון. אמנם מעולם לא באמת ניסיתי לכתוב בעברית בR, אבל ניסיתי להריץ את הקוד שנתת, ויצא לי PDF בלי כותרת בעברית (ריבועים קטנים במקום אותיות). כשהדפסתי למסך היתה כותרת בעברית. כשהדפסתי לPDF, היו אזהרות לרוב מהצורה הבאה:

Warning messages:
1: In title(...) :
  conversion failure on 'שלום עולם' in 'mbcsToSbcs': dot substituted for <d7>

אני עובד על אובונטו.
ה-Sys.getlocale()  נראה ככה:

 "LC_CTYPE=en_US.utf8;LC_NUMERIC=C;LC_TIME=en_US.utf8;LC_COLLATE=en_US.utf8;LC_MONETARY=C;LC_MESSAGES=en_US.utf8;LC_PAPER=en_US.utf8;LC_NAME=C;LC_ADDRESS=C;LC_TELEPHONE=C;LC_MEASUREMENT=en_US.utf8;LC_IDENTIFICATION=C"

זה לא דחוף לי ולא חשוב לי, אבל מסקרן אותי איך לעבוד עם עברית בR... אז כל תובנה תתקבל בברכה (ואולי תתרום לדיון הכללי ותעזור לארי)

עמית

messages.author: a305e65fa9dfb74d
messages.subject: Re: [Israel RUG] Re: R, Hebrew, and PDFs
parts:
This is undoutably a character encoding issue. 
Bottom line- I was unable to solve the problem. Here is what I learned on the way...

Since version 2.10, R uses UTF-8 for internal representation of characters. This is why you should be able to see hebrew on screen and in "standard" plots (say, using the windows device on MS Windows). It will also work in RStudio (I didn't check which graphic device it uses) but not on a Mac using X11 (no text) nor Quartz (inverted hebrew text). Linux will use only X11 so I am not optimistic regarding hebrew plots.
Sadly pdf and postscript devices supported only single-byte encodings, which UTF is not one of them. There are several Hebrew single-bute encodings (say ISO 8859-8). Sadly, I was unable to call them since the encodings available to pdf() and postscript() are the ones with .enc files in the grdevices library. There is no appropriate .enc file for any of the single-byte hebrew encodings. 

All was not lost once I found this:
http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~paul/R/PDF/pdfEncoding.html
Sadly, the simple solution did not work on my Mac (with native cairo) and I didn't try the hard solution. I also tried the Cairo package with the CairoPDF function, without any luck. There is however the hope that it might work on a Linux machine with native Cairo support.

I hope this helped.

J
